1689.dloc: eastcree.org Accent page, sections 'Introduction', 'Accent placement', 'How to accent words', 'Word-final accent' (Southern example rows: maschisin, mitihtimin, takushin/takushinich); Tense Vowels page 'Summary'; DBM 2006 p.1 and footnote 6
1689.heavy: A 'tense' vowel attracts the accent; 'lax' vowels (I, U, or A) do not. The Tense Vowels page lists the tense set as II, UU, AA, WAA, WAAU (historically long; duration variable, e.g. 'II can be longer or shorter in duration'). Southern E occurs in the Southern example rows (chisheyaakw, ishkweshimuwin) but its class is not stated on the fetched pages; Babinski 2018 codes vowel length {short, long} over qualities {a, e, i, u}. Codas play no stated role (Babinski uses open/closed only as a regression covariate).
1689.dflt: Penult and antepenult both lax: 'either vowel might be accented' -- lexically memorized for nouns, no rule found for verbs (not a fixed default).
1689.prule: One accent per word, realized as higher pitch (often also louder); right-edge three-vowel window ('third-last, second-last or last vowel'). Non-final (default, meaning-neutral) accent: on the penult vowel if it is tense (Tense Vowels page lists II, UU, AA, WAA, WAAU); on the antepenult if the antepenult is tense and the penult is lax (I, U, A); if both penult and antepenult are lax, 'either vowel might be accented' -- lexically fixed for nouns (must be memorized; Southern maschisin = antepenult, mitihtimin = penult), no rule discovered for verbs. Monosyllables accent their only vowel; disyllables 'can be accented on the first or last vowel' (no rule given). Final accent is a separate, morphologically meaningful pattern (plural, obviative, etc.). Rule stated once for 'any East Cree word' with parallel Northern and Southern example tables; Babinski 2018 (Southern-only acoustic study, Waskaganish speaker) independently: 'Its stress system is iambic and quantity-sensitive'.
1689.srule: None: 'East Cree words, even long ones, have one ACCENT each'; 'You will normally hear one accent per word in East Cree' -- one pitch accent per word, no secondary or rhythmic stresses described (the secondary accents in Brittain 2000's transcriptions 'do not have phonetic prominence', Dyck, Junker & Logan 2010 fn. 7).

1690.prule: Primary stress on the first (phonemic) vowel of every word of a major category (N, V, A, Adv); the first vowel of a major stem is also stressed (relevant when a directional prefix or reduplicative copy precedes it), and word-internally the first stress is the stronger, later stresses reduced. quantity-insensitive (vowel length is contrastive but plays no role in placement).
1690.srule: Placed by morphology, not rhythm: when a directional prefix or a reduplicative copy precedes the stem, the stem-initial vowel is also stressed and Stress Reduction makes the first stress in the word primary and the later one reduced (líl+kəṭà+n+c̓+t 'he chased them into the corral', bək̓ó+bk̓ò+l+t 'the bird pecks all the time', máṭmmàt 'he lay down'); words without such a prefix or copy have one stress. No alternating secondary stress described.

Note 1 (p.92): 'Data for this paper was compiled over a three year period while the author was living in the village of Bosadi. Many informants were used in collecting the data.' morph.stmt: Suena is exclusively suffixing/postposing: 'All relators are postpositionals' (Wilson 1974 §5.6.1 p.24), nouns 'can be affixed [with suffixes -ra, -re, -ka, -wa, -e] to show possession, endearment, definiteness, coordination, Indirect Object, and Location' (§5.2 p.17), and 'Verbs are composed of up to six tagmemes. In order they are: Root, Vowel, Grammatical Function, Person, Mood, Number' with Person, Mood and Number 'always the last three slots on the verb' (§5.13 p.58); the only non-suffixal morphology is left-edge CV reduplication (plural/intensive, continuative stems) and preverbal free negators oko/kaka. No prefix of any kind is described.

1711.dq: The speakers are aware of word stress and use this feature to create riddles by putting the stress on the wrong syllable to cause the hearer to misunderstand the utterance. 1711.prule: Lexical, unpredictable word stress; any syllable may be stressed in 2- and 3-syllable words (final least frequent in trisyllables); in 4-syllable words the final is never stressed and the initial only rarely; 5-syllable words stress only penult or antepenult. No influence of syllable shape; long vowels need not carry stress but the stressed syllable is at most one syllable removed from a long vowel.
1711.srule: Exists but placement not given: 'Words with four and more syllables may also carry a secondary stress on another syllable' (the 4- and 5-syllable example lists mark one stress per word). In reduplicated derived stems the first element's stress 'is echoed in a weaker form on the second element' (CV́CV-C̣VCV).

1712.srule: Secondary word-accent is placed by morphology, not by syllable count: prefixes and reduplication syllables often carry it (nà-pútol, sù-súlat 'will write', nà-rì-rinìg) and in certain suffixal formations it falls on the initial syllable of the underlying word (alìs -> àlís-an), dropped when that syllable is closed (luksò -> luksú-han); purely rhythmic stresses on runs of unstressed syllables are variable and never distinctive (Bloomfield 1917 secs. 40, 43-44, 50, 338). Schachter & Reid 2008 do not mention secondary stress. Later work (French 1988 ch. 3; French 1991; Zuraw & Roca 2025 sec. 8) adds that pre-tonic closed and long-vowelled syllables (e.g. aspect reduplicants) attract secondary stress, subject to clash avoidance before a stressed penult; no acoustic study of secondary stress exists (Zuraw & Roca 2025: 20).

1713.prule: Stress is anchored to the stem syllable of the Athabaskan (prefixing) word: 'the stem syllable is always stressed' is the predominant pattern, stated as a 'strong tendency' that is absolute in nouns and has exceptions only in verbs (c. 88% stem stress in four-syllable words); main stress is the LAST stressed syllable of the word in 85% of the corpus (315/370), i.e. normally the stem syllable (word-final, or penultimate before a -V suffix/enclitic). Position is set by morphological structure, not by syllable count or weight ('morphological factors may take precedence over phonological factors').
1713.srule: There is always a stressed syllable before the stem syllable, so a single pre-stem syllable carries secondary stress in clash with the stem primary (ò ó: mè-lá, kà#ts'ét); with more than one pre-stem syllable, secondary stress falls on alternating syllables counting back from the stem syllable (ò o ó o ùdin-úda, o ò o ó udèθi-dlét); the enclitic ʔeʔè: takes secondary stress after a stem primary (…ó o o ò#). Analysed as syllabic trochees built right-to-left, final foot = main stress; residue: word-initial òò ~3%, two unstressed syllables in a row ~12% (word-final 'troughs').

1715.prule: No lexical/word stress.
